newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Gore sets U.S. themes for Earth Summit.
newsitem.headline: Gore sets U.S. themes for Earth Summit.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore on Monday spelled out themes the United States will push at the United Nation's Earth Summit, rejecting calls for a new treaty to protect forests and stopping short of specific targets to cut global warming despite European pressure.

In opening remarks at the conference, which will assess progress since the first Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro five years ago, Gore spoke in upbeat terms about technology's ability to help mankind cope with environmental problems.
But he said many of Rio's promises, such as reducing heat-trapping pollution, were unfulfilled.

"Today greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise at record rates. Unless we change course, during the lives of our grandchildren the concentration of these gases in the atmosphere will reach levels not seen on this planet for more than 50 million years," he said.

Gore spoke after the Group of Seven industrialised nations summit in Denver, where European nations blasted the United States for refusing to agree specific targets for reducing fossil fuel emissions that cause global warming.

The United States still has not announced the targets it will seek in climate change negotiations, set to culminate in December in Kyoto, Japan. However Washington says it cannot agree to the steep cuts the Europeans want because of the impact on U.S. industry.
"Kyoto presents a critical opportunity for the world to forge an agreement with binding emissions limits, flexibility in meeting those targets and the participation of all nations," Gore said.
Gore also indicated the United States is set to clash with the Europeans and other countries on forest issues.

While a number of countries led by the European Union, Malaysia and Canada are pushing for a new treaty to protect forests, the United States is leading other nations that feel new negotiations would simply waste time.
"We must work to protect the world's forests by creating a follow-up mechanism to the intergovernmental panel on forests that produces on-the-ground results, not new negotiations," Gore said.
